explain.say: On the night of 22 August 1791, enslaved people on the northern plain of Saint-Domingue, a French Caribbean colony, rose up. Tradition links it to a gathering at Bois Caïman days before. Thirteen years later they had defeated France and founded Haiti, the first nation born from a successful revolt of enslaved people. Look at the timeline.

explain.say: Look at the sizes for 1789. About 465,000 enslaved people, about 31,000 white colonists and about 28,000 free people of colour. Saint-Domingue grew a huge share of Europe's sugar and coffee, and so many enslaved people died from overwork that planters kept buying more. What does this imbalance tell you about how the colony was held together?

explain.say: Now the map. Toussaint Louverture, born enslaved, became the revolution's great general. He fought Spanish and British invaders and by 1801 ruled the colony. France had abolished slavery in 1794, pushed by the revolt. In 1802 Napoleon sent an army to restore control; Toussaint was seized and died in a French prison. Why do you think Napoleon wanted the colony back?

The fighting went on under Jean-Jacques Dessalines. Yellow fever and fierce resistance destroyed the French army, beaten at Vertières in November 1803. On 1 January 1804 Dessalines declared independence and took the Taíno name Haiti. In 1804 he also ordered the killing of most remaining French colonists, an episode historians still weigh. See independence light up.

explain.say: Watch the chain. Napoleon's defeat helped push him to sell Louisiana to the United States. Haiti was isolated, and in 1825 France demanded 150 million francs to recognise it, a debt that lasted into the twentieth century. C. L. R. James and Michel-Rolph Trouillot showed how long this revolution was silenced. Wonderful work. Challenge: why might it have seemed unthinkable to Europeans then?

faq.a: The revolt that began in August 1791 among enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue. It ended slavery there, defeated French, Spanish and British forces, and created the independent state of Haiti on 1 January 1804.
asks: When did the Haitian Revolution start?

faq.a: A formerly enslaved man who became the revolution's leading general and governor of the colony by 1801. Arrested by Napoleon's forces in 1802, he died in prison at Fort de Joux in France in April 1803.

faq.q: Why did Haiti have to pay France?
faq.a: In 1825 France demanded an indemnity of 150 million francs, later reduced to 90 million, as the price of recognising Haiti, backed by warships. Haiti borrowed to pay, and the debt burdened it into the twentieth century.
Toussaint's lieutenant, born enslaved, who led the final war against the French and declared Haiti's independence in 1804. He became its first ruler and was assassinated in 1806.

faq.q: How many enslaved people lived in Saint-Domingue?
faq.a: About 465,000 in 1789, compared with about 31,000 white colonists and about 28,000 free people of colour. Many had been born in Africa, because deaths were so high that planters kept importing captives.

facts: France abolished slavery in its colonies in February 1794; Napoleon restored it elsewhere in 1802.
In 1825 France demanded an indemnity of 150 million francs from Haiti.
